body: Is there an existing proposal about this?

> Is there an existing proposal about this?

I'm not aware of a proposal for adding script components specifically. However, there are a handful of proposals that are relevant as they have the same or similar use cases that script components can address.

https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/4872

https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/6416

Tbh I don't see the pr can make any critical sense to Godot users, because the component system (i mean multiscript system) greatly breaks the design philosophy of Godot.
BTW if this is really necessary, this can completely be implemented as an addon, as a GDScript can be instantiated by other scripts and you can establish a system (singleton) that manages component scripts of single node. 
Meanwhile you can store the component scripts into a metadata and you can get them from the meta.

> Tbh I don't see the pr can make any critical sense to Godot users, because the component system (i mean multiscript system) greatly breaks the design philosophy of Godot

I'm not sure Godot's lack of editor-friendly way to do composition is a design philosophy rather than an oversight because it hinders engine's ability to scale to teams that have anyone besides programmers in them.

An artist or a game designer needs to be able to easily put together components provided by a programmer to create new behaviors and experiment with game mechanics without touching any code. Same game designer then needs to be able to join another team at another job and still be able to do it without going through a lengthy briefing on how components are done there (is it child nodes? is it metadata? is it an array with component resources?). When you buy assets from the asset store, for the sake of your own sanity their components need to be done in the same way everywhere so that you could just start using them in your projects without reading docs or looking at the code. An established way to do composition at the engine level would also make it easier for one asset to check for components of another asset so that your different asset store purchases from different people could work together.

There are some limitations to using child nodes as components that keep coming up every now and then, for example having to enable editable children to be able to change exported variables on components, but it goes beyond that

Reinventing composition in every team is a waste of everyone's time. This needs a proposal.

> I'm not sure Godot's lack of editor-friendly way to do composition is a design philosophy rather than an oversight because it hinders engine's ability to scale to teams that have anyone besides programmers in them.

Iirc there is already a proposal about supporting multiscript system for single node:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/discussions/5609
where maybe you can find the reason why this feature was removed and single script is supported.

> There are some limitations to using child nodes as components that keep coming up every now and then, for example having to enable editable children to be able to change exported variables on components, but it goes beyond that.

Yeah, I'd admit that nodes as components does lead to some flaws and inconvenience, however, multiple scripts in the same node would greatly breaks the compatibility with previous versions, which should be cautiously considered. Another reason is that multiple scripts would cause "referencing problems", e.g.:
```gdscript
# Component A
extends Node

var a = 1

# Component B
extends Node

var a = "hello"
```
In this case, which `a` would you like to reference, if you don't try to reference the corresponding component first? Futher talking, even if the component were implemented, we don't have generic type currently in GDScript, so for GDScripters they should cast the component first to the component type they want, which would silently increase the length of code.

> Reinventing composition in every team is a waste of everyone's time. This needs a proposal.

Yes, the prs the author linked are **not about components**, but **traits**. Trait is a syntactic GDScript-oriented way to support component system, while this pr supports in the whole engine, which are targeting different aspects.
So, @RudyFisher7 you (next time) need a *real proposal for this feature*, instead of linking the ones that you didn't get the critical point.

> however, multiple scripts in the same node would greatly breaks the compatibility with previous versions, which should be cautiously considered

I agree. This PR is a good conversation starter about the larger issue of composition in Godot, but I didn't leave any comment on the solution itself because I acknowledge that this might not be the best way of addressing this.

I think improving the existing system (child node components) is fine as long as the engine addresses all of its current problems and endorses a certain predictable way of doing it (via docs and examples) that the community agrees on. Because while it's great that Godot allows you to do the same thing in a lot of different ways, in the larger context of third-party assets and big teams it's clear that there needs to be an established editor-friendly way to go about logic reusability and interfacing. So there needs to be a bigger discussion about that.

Edit: Apologies, [this message](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/105663#issuecomment-2824131553) wasn't loaded while writing the comment, so some points might be outdated.

@passivestar 

>  for example having to enable editable children to be able to change exported variables on components, but it goes beyond that

Doesn't this belong to an enhancement to the `PackedScene editing workflow` that's nice to have? How is it related to the `multi-script` system?

Your example can be easily resolved by introducing `auto-children editing` (enable `editable children` when unfolding the packed scene node instance).

> Reinventing composition in every team is a waste of everyone's time.

This is incorrect. Composition does exist, and you can freely compose by combining Node children, as the Node itself is the Component. There isn't any fundamental difference between Godot and other engines that treat Script as a Component.

```Godot Engine
Node00 <-- MainScript01
 |-- Node02
 |-- Node <-- Script03
 |-- Node04
 |-- Node <-- Script05
 |-- Node06 <-- MainScript07
      |-- Node08
      |-- Node <-- Script09
      |-- Node10
      |-- Node <-- Script11
```

```Engine treat Scripts as Component
Object00
 |-- MainScriptComponent01
 |-- Component02
 |-- ScriptComponent03
 |-- Component04
 |-- ScriptComponent05
 |-- Object06
      |-- MainScriptComponent07
      |-- Component08
      |-- ScriptComponent09
      |-- Component10
      |-- ScriptComponent11
```

> An artist or a game designer needs to be able to easily put together components provided by a programmer to create new behaviors and experiment with game mechanics without touching any code. Same game designer then needs to be able to join another team at another job and still be able to do it without going through a lengthy briefing on how components are done there (is it child nodes? is it metadata? is it an array with component resources?). When you buy assets from the asset store, for the sake of your own sanity their components need to be done in the same way everywhere so that you could just start using them in your projects without reading docs or looking at the code. An established way to do composition at the engine level would also make it easier for one asset to check for components of another asset so that your different asset store purchases from different people could work together.

This paragraph is true for all existing Engines, you may need to elaborate on how Godot Engine does it wrong, and why introducing multi-script system can resolve it.

This example doesn't represent a component system as they usually are designed in engines. Here, components are resources attached like metadata, but have a more specialized workflow and validation system than metadata. I acknowledge there used to be multiple scripts allowed, however they were implemented differently and in a way that was more difficult to maintain in the engine.

Another critical factor is the performance overhead of splitting up logic among multiple Nodes in the tree and adding more and more Nodes. The documentation discusses this. This PR was the result of me running into the limitations that the attached proposals found, finding my SceneTree growing as more child scenes with many Node "components" were spawned and performance was becoming a concern, and wanting a workflow that allowed me to directly edit the exported properties of the child scene components at design time. This flavor of script component (or if you want to say mutliscript) system seems to solve these problems for my projects.

> So, @RudyFisher7 you (next time) need a *real proposal for this feature*, instead of linking the ones that you didn't get the critical point.

Respectfully, I disagree that this PR misses the critical points of these proposals. I do acknowledge that the community called for traits or interfaces and not components, and giving components instead would probably not sit well with the community. However, I personally believe a component system similar to this implementation (though probably 1 that is cleaner and allows querying based on base classes as well maybe...) solves many if not all of their use cases/limitations without needing to do a lot of work to add the feature to GDScript as a language feature via traits or interfaces. It also uses a familiar scripting API to the Node API (get_node, get_component, etc.).

There are several community projects that do use metadata to essentially get "get_component()" and "has_component()"/"has_interface()" type of queries. I was also using this. But there are still limitations to this, as components don't handle the Node notifications unless the components are also Nodes themselves. The queries are also less performant.

Anyway, I appreciate most of the discussion around this as I've felt I've been silently observing the traits/interfaces discussion with this idea as a low effort solution for quite some time. I acknowledge that this type of component system hasn't really been discussed much in the community and so might be confusing to most users as to why it's even being added, as well as the current implementation might be a little naive and in need of more fleshing out if nothing else.

[Edit]

I also acknowledge that this implementation is in contrast to Godot's Node based design. However, I think having both script components and the Nodes available leads to a lot of flexibility for users. If users don't want to use the components, they don't need to, and they also don't pay for their existence.

> This paragraph is true for all existing Engines, you may need to elaborate on how Godot Engine does it wrong

To answer the question of where Godot's support for composition is lacking specifically (without getting into the multi-script discussion) some of the issues that come to mind are:
- There's no good established way to check for a component's existence. `Node.find_child()` cannot search by type, unlike i.e `GetComponent<>()` in Unity. This for example makes it more clunky to check for a component on something that you got via a raycast, or to simply check for a sibling of a certain type that might not exist. You can make your own helper function (or get nodes by name if you can) but it makes it less likely for people to create composable systems and more likely to resort to more coupled ones. Part of the appeal of composition is that components can be made optional, which opens a lot of possibilities for experimenting with game mechanics in editor without touching code, which in turn makes the engine more team-friendly
- Poor workflow for adjusting variables on nested components as I mentioned before, could be solved either the way you suggested or some other way
- No nice way for one component to require another component's existence, this is due to the limitations of godot's configuration warning system. If you want warnings you need to make your component a `@tool` which requires early returns in every lifecycle method to prevent running them in editor. Unity has a `[RequireComponent()]` attribute that adds required components automatically. Godot would need a way to selectively run code in editor to fix the warning system
- While Godot technically supports composition via nodes, there aren't many examples from Godot itself. In Unity, since components are first-class every code example no matter how small is made out of components, with components referencing each other by type, so it scales reasonably well. If you look through Godot demo projects repo you'll see that since the examples are simple, nodes usually reference each other via hardcoded node paths (and often their code is simple enough for them to not even need to reference each other at all because they only use engine's APIs). However when the project grows, the task of structuring it in a way that would be modular and team-friendly falls entirely on the user. I think it's nice that Godot is simple out of the box, but perhaps it would help for it to at least include some demo project that would show the community how to structure their games/plugins in a way that scales beyond solo projects

I don't think having both is a good idea, having two different ways to do components would become a problem for Godot's plugin ecosystem. It's also best when user components and engine components are done the same way, and Godot's own components are nodes (i.e physics colliders)

> To answer the question of where Godot's support for composition is lacking specifically (without getting into the multi-script discussion) some of the issues that come to mind are...

Overall supported, with the following can be implemented as separate features:
`GetComponent<>()` can be simply implemented as the following in C#, so what's lacking for GDScript is the proper support of `Type` type.
```csharp
public static T? GetChildOfType<T>(this Node node) where T : Node =>
        (T?)node.GetChildren().FirstOrDefault(x => x is T);
```

`[RequireComponent()]` can be implemented as an extra script property alongside the `class_name`.
```gdscript
class_name MyClass
required_child [AnimatedSprite2D, AnimatedBody2D, Area2D] # +
extends Node
```

> > I also acknowledge that this implementation is in contrast to Godot's Node based design. However, I think having both script components and the Nodes available leads to a lot of flexibility for users. If users don't want to use the components, they don't need to, and they also don't pay for their existence

> I don't think having both is a good idea, having two different ways to do components would become a problem for Godot's plugin ecosystem. It's also best when user components and engine components are done the same way, and Godot's own components are nodes (i.e physics colliders)

I think there's a better way I could have put this...

Nodes still offer the functionality (colliders, etc.), these Components would simply implement the logic that manages the Nodes' functionality. Applied to one of the examples in the linked proposal on traits, a Tree3D scene is made of a StaticBody3D (offers collision functionality). This could have a BurnableComponent (implements logic that uses StaticBody3D to sense if fire is touching it). Perhaps some Tree3Ds also need a FarmableComponent (senses when an Axe3D collides with it). Using Components instead of full-blown Nodes for this "glue" logic is hopefully lighter weight and nicer to manage in the inspector since they're grouped together and can all be on a scene's root Node.

Where extending Nodes could be handy is when, say, StaticBody3D needs added custom physics functionality.

An \@required_components/children annotation would be nice too. One solution has been to use assert(child != null) inside _ready(), but is of course only checked during runtime.

This is quite an interesting PR you have put together here! I could definitely see this kind of feature being of interest, at least to some groups.

As others have pointed out, this is a rather large feature, and adding it would have quite an impact on Godot. Please put together a [Godot Implementation Proposal](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/new?template=feature_proposal.yml) that describes the feature and what it would be useful for. 

Whether the feature should be added or not should be discussed on the proposal page, not here.

_(side note: I can also see this being material for a GDExtension, although it would probably need additions to GDExtension's APIs to make it work. This is also something that can be discussed on a proposal page.)_

A lot of people already use Actor as a class, Could you rename this class to be something that better fits or is more relevant. If this is merged it would break a lot of projects or cause warnings as folks would inadvertently hide this class.
